Q: SQL Server hint NOLOCK and ROWLOCK A:

As barry already explained, these two hints can complement each other, but they are typically used in different contexts and to solve different resource contention issues.

The WITH (NOLOCK) tells the server to employ READ UNCOMMITTED transaction isolation level, which means you are exposed to the risk of reading uncommitted ("dirty") rows which may be subsequently rolled back and thus have never existed. It does prevent classic deadlocks on reads, but at the expense of getting invalid data.

If there is a chance GetUser or CheckPassword operations may access the profile of the user being updated through UpdateUser operation, then WITH (NOLOCK) is not recommended to use.

The WITH (ROWLOCK) table hint can be used with either SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements, to instruct the server to only apply a Range-Lock(s) on the rows being modified or added, and to avoid escalating the lock to page or table level. The rest of rows are not locked and can be accessed by another query.

However, if the default transaction isolation level at the SQL Server is READ COMMITTED or more restrictive, and SNAPSHOT READS are not enabled, then an active INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE transaction may still block the SELECT query, if lookup conditions match or overlap.

Use the hint when only a single or only a few rows will be affected by the query, to keep the lock from locking rows that will not be deleted by the query. That will let another query read unrelated rows at the same time instead of having to wait for the delete to complete.

If you use it on a query that will delete a lot of rows, it may degrade the performance as the database will try to avoid escalating the locks to a larger scope, even if it would have been more efficient.

Q: Minimum hardware requirements for running Raspberry Pi OS on VirtualBox A:

Your configuration borders on the side of a bit shallow, seeing this guide here issues 2GB, 1 CPU and 10GB of disk as the smallest possible requirement, because some older Raspberry Pis did have a similar amount of resources, however for smooth usage with a lot of programs, you'd be better sticking with a bit more.

Seeing this forum post others say a similar configuration to yours is fine, so yeah, I think you'll be fine, but you might run out of disk space for example if you're dealing with a large amount of programs, and obviously - the more the merrier.

Q: Should Hudi metadata fields (e.g., _hoodie_commit_time) be dropped when transforming data from ODS to DWD? A:

Yes, it is. You're correct, by leaving the internal metadata fields you risk a schema conflict should anything change, you might mess with primary/foreign keys and the relations involved with these tables, so to drop them with something like this:


val metadataCols = odsDf.columns.filter(_.startsWith("_hoodie_"))
val cleanedDf = odsDf.drop(metadataCols: _*)

Makes the most sense.

Q: C++ Error "Variable-sized object may not be initialized A:

The error implies that nodes is not a compile time constant which is a requirement for defining arrays in standard C++. A valid C++ example:

constexpr std::size_t nodes = 10;
bool visited[nodes]{};

There is also some differences between the two arrays.

This would define an array of nodes amount of vector<bool>s. Each vector<bool> could (had variable length arrays been valid C++) then grow and shrink dynamically (if this is std::vector and not some other kind of vector):

vector<bool> visited[nodes] = {0};

This would define an array of bools (again, had variable length arrays been valid C++):

bool visited[nodes] = {0};

Variable length arrays is however not standard C++. They exist in C, but not even in C can you use an initializer. Well, since C23 you can, but it has to be empty:

bool visited[nodes] = {};

In C++, you'd use one the std::vector constructor taking a count to initialize it to hold the number of bools you want:

std::vector<bool> visited(nodes);        // nodes number of default-inserted (false) bools
std::vector<bool> visited(nodes, false); // nodes number of copy constructed bools

Some C++ implementations do accept variable length arrays as an extension and some even accept them with an initializer:

bool visited[nodes] = {false}; // accepted by gcc as an extension

I suggest that you learn to use the standard C++ containers, like std::vector instead.

Be aware though: std::vector<bool> is often specialized to occupy as little memory as possible. That means it will pack the bools with as many it can fit in a byte. That means, it usually fits 8 bools in one byte (but on some platforms even more). This makes it a bit odd to work with and a bit slower than one would expect in some situations.

Q: Some quest For my project about ddd golang A:

Put it in the scrapper application layer, not in domain and not in bot.

Why:

  • domain should contain business rules, not Telegram-specific text formatting

  • bot should stay thin and only send already prepared messages

  • infra should deal with transport/adapters, not with building message content

A good option is something like:

application/scrapper/notifications
application/scrapper/out/bot

So the flow is:

domain event/entity -> application formatter/presenter -> bot DTO/command -> bot sends message

In other words, treat it as an application-level mapper/presenter for an outbound integration contract. This keeps the domain clean and the bot decoupled from scrapper internals.
